leonardo-01.title: Presence is constructed, not captured

evidence.claim: The Louvre identifies the sitter as Lisa Gherardini and records the painting on a poplar panel.
evidence.limit: Identity does not tell us what she was thinking.

evidence.claim: Thin transitions make the face less sharply bounded than the silhouette of the hands.
evidence.limit: This is our comparison of visible effects, not a quotation from Leonardo.

evidence.claim: The transparent veil is visible, but appearance alone does not establish its social meaning.
evidence.limit: The linked object record supports identification and material context. This entry does not attribute a pregnancy, mourning narrative or named scholarly dispute to that record.

description: Composition
A seated woman turns toward the viewer, her joined hands low in the image. Her upper body forms a broad, stable mass.
Space and light
A ledge separates her from distant winding water, roads and rocky terrain. The face is softly illuminated; the eyes, mouth and veil have delicate boundaries.
Handling
Gradual changes in tone differ from the more legible edges of clothing and hands. A digital reproduction can obscure the thinnest transitions.
technique: A wood panel supplies a rigid support; its identity comes from the object record, not from the photograph.
Thin, translucent paint transitions soften the modeling. Compare a cheek with a hand rather than treating every edge as equally dissolved.
Oxidized varnish affects present color. Our screen reproduction is not a reconstruction of the original palette.
provenance: The Louvre records the work as formerly belonging to the French Crown.
The object record gives 1793 as the museum acquisition date.

room.caption: Conceptual domestic encounter: a person meets a relatively small panel. Original furnishings and hanging height are not reconstructed.

reception.text: The Louvre traces early admiration, copies and later literary mythmaking. These are different stages of reputation, not evidence of a single timeless response.
Can you look at the structure of a portrait already surrounded by expectations?

leonardo-02.title: A wall that answers a room

evidence.claim: The work occupies the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan.

source.title: Museo del Cenacolo Vinciano · The Last Supper

evidence.limit: Its current museum access is not the original experience of communal dining.

evidence.claim: Leonardo worked on dry wall rather than using the standard wet-plaster fresco process.

source.title: Museo del Cenacolo Vinciano · The Last Supper

evidence.limit: Do not use a generic fresco diagram to explain this painting.

evidence.claim: The central stillness is intensified by the reactions around it.

source.title: Museo del Cenacolo Vinciano · The Last Supper

evidence.limit: Gestures support an argument about composition, not access to the apostles’ private thoughts.

description: Composition
Thirteen men sit or gather behind a long table. The central figure is framed by a distant opening; the others lean, turn and gesture in clustered groups.
Space and light
Ceiling and side-wall lines narrow toward the center. The table forms a horizontal barrier across the foreground.
Handling and condition
The surface is uneven and interrupted by losses. The surviving image and its conservation history must be considered together.
technique: The painting begins with an architectural wall, not a portable canvas.
A dry-wall process gave Leonardo scope to work gradually; it also differs materially from pigment binding into wet plaster.
The surviving surface has experienced damage and conservation. A complete-looking reproduction is not proof of an untouched surface.
provenance: The mural remains tied to the Milanese refectory for which it was made.

rembrandt-01.title: The commission becomes an event

evidence.claim: Technical research revealed an underlying painted sketch.
evidence.limit: A research image detects materials; it is not a photograph of an earlier complete painting.

evidence.claim: The sketch uses a light, chalk-rich paint over a brown ground.
evidence.limit: This finding concerns this object; it is not a universal recipe for Rembrandt.

evidence.claim: Illumination assigns unequal prominence within the company.
evidence.limit: Unequal visibility is not proof of dissatisfaction among the sitters.

description: Composition
A crowded armed company fills an architectural setting. A dark-clothed officer with a red sash and a pale-clothed officer lead the foreground.
Space and light
Bright patches pick out faces, cloth and a smaller girl among much darker figures. Weapons and raised arms cross the gathering.
Handling
Differences in finish and brightness compete with the density of bodies. The painting demands movement of the eye rather than a single scan along a row.
technique: A prepared canvas carries a brown ground.
Technical examination identifies a light painted compositional sketch beneath the visible surface.
Subsequent painting changes and elaborates that arrangement. A diagram is a reading aid, not a replacement for technical imaging.
provenance: A civic guard company commissioned the group portrait for an Amsterdam assembly setting.
The painting was trimmed for a new placement. An early copy helps researchers discuss the missing margins.

room.caption: Conceptual public hall: a large commissioned group portrait addresses a room. This is not a measured reconstruction of the Kloveniersdoelen.

reception.text: The discovery of an underlying sketch changes the evidence available for discussing planning and revision.
What does a group portrait owe to its individual subjects—and what can it do as a painting?

description: Composition
A young figure turns her head over a shoulder toward the viewer. The face, pale collar and earring emerge against a nearly dark field.
Clothing and light
Blue and yellow fabric wraps the head. The brown jacket is described more broadly than the softly modeled face.
Handling
Highlights on lips and earring are sharply concentrated. Much of the face is built through gradual transitions rather than explicit outlines.
technique: A canvas support and prepared layers precede the visible image.
The face and clothing are handled differently; soft modeling need not imply equal finish throughout.
Research into altered layers helps explain why the present dark field is not a secure guide to the original background.
provenance: The museum describes substantial gaps in the early ownership history.
Arnoldus Andries des Tombe purchased the painting in 1881; it entered the Mauritshuis through his bequest in 1903.

van-gogh-01.title: Observation becomes a constructed night

evidence.claim: MoMA dates the painting to June 1889 at Saint-Rémy.
evidence.limit: The record does not prove that every depicted feature was visible at one moment.

evidence.claim: The painting was made in daytime sessions and combines observed and invented features.
evidence.limit: It should not be described as a literal nocturnal snapshot.

evidence.claim: The cypress links the landscape and sky through its rising shape.
evidence.limit: This relationship does not diagnose a medical condition or establish a single symbol.

description: Composition
A large blue night sky occupies most of the canvas. Circular stars and a crescent moon glow above a compact village and low hills.
Space and movement
A dark cypress rises close to the left edge. The church steeple repeats a smaller vertical within the village.
Handling
Short directional strokes curve around bright forms and run across the land. Geometric roofs contrast with the sky’s broad movement.
technique: Oil paint on canvas allows a visible, directional handling of the surface.
Short marks articulate forms while also making the eye travel along the painted surface.
Daytime work, memory and observation contribute to the construction. Visible energy is not evidence of an unplanned or instantaneous execution.
provenance: Made during Van Gogh’s stay at Saint-Rémy.
MoMA records acquisition through the Lillie P. Bliss Bequest, by exchange.

room.caption: Conceptual easel painting: a constructed image can be developed apart from the time and conditions it depicts. This does not reconstruct Van Gogh’s room.

reception.voice: Van Gogh · a short excerpt from a letter, English translation cited by MoMA
reception.text: “the morning star, which looked very big”
A remembered observation supplies evidence for a starting point, not a key that translates every mark into a biographical message.
